youtube.title: C++ Lambdas with STL Algorithms | C++ Programming EP 78
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a lambda, sort with your own rule and capture a variable in a lambda, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Lambdas with algorithms · 1:15 Sort descending and count_if · 2:25 Anatomy of a lambda · 3:01 Second program · 4:13 Recap · 4:43 Bug of the Day · 5:31 Challenge · 5:51 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we hand rules to algorithms. A lambda is a small function you write in the same place where you use it.

scenes.onScreen: "Lambdas with algorithms": numbered lines (1. A lambda is a function with no name; 2. Square brackets hold the captures; 3. Algorithms accept lambdas as rules) and an analogy card: a sticky note with a small rule, handed to the algorithm
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A lambda has square brackets, a parameter list and a body. The square brackets are the capture list. They name outside variables that the lambda may read. Think of a sticky note with a small rule. You hand the note to the algorithm, and it follows the rule. Many algorithms take a rule as the last argument. The rule says how to compare, or what to count. A lambda is the best way to write the rule. Write the lambda right where you need it. The reader sees the rule next to the call, and does not have to jump to another place.
points: A lambda is a function with no name

analogy.title: Lambdas with algorithms
analogy.body: A sticky note with a small rule, handed to the algorithm

scenes.onScreen: lambda.cpp: a lambda sorts in reverse and another lambda counts big numbers
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 8] The empty square brackets mean the lambda captures nothing. It takes two ints. [HL 8] It says that a comes first when a is bigger. The result is nine seven five two one. [HL 13] Now we make a local variable. [HL 14] Putting limit in the brackets captures it. The lambda can now read it. [HL 14] Count if counts the items for which the lambda says true. Three items are bigger than four. [HL 8] The third argument is a lambda that takes two ints. It returns true when a is bigger than b. This changes sort from smallest first to biggest first. [HL 13] The variable limit is four. [HL 14] The capture list holds limit, so the lambda can read it. Count if counts the numbers above four. The answer is three.

scenes.onScreen: a table that names each part of a lambda
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: A lambda has three parts. The capture list names outside variables. The parameters are the values the algorithm passes in. The body holds the rule. Notice the two jobs. The lambda in sort decides the order of two items. The lambda in count if answers a yes or no question about one item. The algorithm calls the lambda again and again.

diagram.caption: a table that names each part of a lambda
rows: outside variables the lambda may read

scenes.onScreen: students.cpp: students are sorted by marks with a lambda
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 7] A student has a name and marks. [HL 14] We sort the students. [HL 14] The lambda compares marks, so the highest marks come first. [HL 15] For each calls a lambda on every item. [HL 15] The lambda prints Asha ninety-one, then Mia eighty-five, then Ravi seventy-eight. [HL 13] This vector holds three students. [HL 14] The lambda compares the marks, so the students are ordered by their marks, highest first. [HL 15] For each runs a lambda on every student. It prints the name and the marks.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as students dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints the three students, from the highest marks to the lowest. Notice the order of the output. Asha has ninety-one, Mia has eighty-five, and Ravi has seventy-eight.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A lambda is a small function with no name. Two. The capture list names outside variables. Three. Algorithms take lambdas as rules. Four. Pass a struct by const reference to avoid a copy. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A lambda is a small function with no name.
The capture list names outside variables.
Pass a struct by const reference to avoid a copy.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A variable that is not captured
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The lambda reads limit, but the brackets are empty. The compiler says limit is not captured. Put limit in the square brackets. A lambda starts with a clean slate. It sees nothing from outside until you capture it. Write the name in the square brackets to copy it. Add an ampersand to use the original variable, and to change it.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the lambda join the party? Nobody had to give it a name.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the lambda join the party? Nobody had to give it a name.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: count the even numbers
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Use count if and a lambda to count the even numbers in a vector. Hint: the lambda tests the remainder after dividing by two. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: ranges in C plus plus twenty. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

capture.cpp: In lambda function:
capture.cpp:9:67: error: 'limit' is not captured
    9 |     int big = count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x) { return x > limit; });
      |                                                                   ^~~~~
capture.cpp:9:45: note: the lambda has no capture-default
    9 |     int big = count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x) { return x > limit; });
bug.why: A lambda cannot see local variables unless you capture them. Write the name in the square brackets. Use an ampersand in front of the name to capture by reference.

pun: "Why did the lambda join the party? Nobody had to give it a name."
challenge: Use count if and a lambda to count the even numbers in a vector. Hint: the lambda tests the remainder after dividing by two.
challengeAnswer: Call count if with begin and end. The lambda takes an int x and returns x modulo two equals zero.
